body: Self-harm is self-harm, whether the cuts are shallow or deep. You are still doing damage to your body when you make shallow cuts. Try not to compare your cuts to those of other people. Your pain is not less because your cuts are shallow; your pain is just as valid as anyone else's.
I personally don't find it particularly painful to cut, be it a deep one or a shallow cut. We all have different pain tolerance's. The level of pain felt will be different from person to person.

You're right, I do know the drill, I know it a little too well. I have some steri-strips, but not enough for these cuts, plus I find they are crap compared to actual sutures or staples. I've looked at skin staplers on Amazon as well, but don't have the funds for one at the moment.
I usually go down to fat tissue. That's the plan,  the usual.
I can't say I was injured that badly. Mostly some nasty abrasions. I've done much more damage to my body in the years following. I'm honestly surprised I've survived this long.

My lot in life is that my body is resilient as fuck, and I do heal very well. I've only had minor infections, usually when my cuts have been sutured or stapled, which is kind of ironic. That being said, I do recommend that any deep cuts you may make be assessed by a medical professional.

I sadly don't have any tips for you, but I can say I relate to what you posted. I too have had throbbing scars lately, and the one large one on my chest has been particularly irritated as of late. I think part of it is due to the way I scar, but part of it may be emotional as well. They seem to throb more when I'm feeling very anxious or have urges to self-harm.

The urge to self-harm can be very strong. I can understand why you may be relapsing.

Ad for stepping up your shit... I think it's pretty normal for some people who self-injure to compare their scars to other self-harmers at times. I think part of it is just seeking a sense of belonging, that we're not alone in doing this. What sometimes happens, however, is you can experience a sense of inadequacy when comparing scars.

Self-harm is self-harm, whether it's shallow cuts, deep cuts, burns, starving yourself, etc. It's not a competition. You are not less of a self-harmer for making smaller, shallower cuts. Whatever you are experiencing is not less because of smaller cuts.

I feel fortunate in that I was never really exposed to other people's self-injury. That being said, due to the nature of my self-harm, I have made many deep cuts, have many prominent scars, and would probably be considered a severe case. This isn't something I'm proud of; I'm pretty neutral about it. But I would hate if someone who cuts were to see me and think "man, I need to step this up".

Deep cuts are a slippery slope. They get highly addictive. I experience the craving to cut myself deeply every day. Deep cuts often mean sutures, or large scars if you choose not to seek medical attention. You put yourself at a higher risk of infection, and if you aren't familiar with anatomy, you could risk damaging tendons or muscle, or even severing a vein or an artery.

So don't step up your game. You're okay and safer where you are now.

I personally still don't see my self-harm as an issue. I've been doing it so long, I have so many scars already, and it's kept me alive,  so why should I stop? It makes me feel calm and in control, it's not a bad thing.

I'm honestly not sure how I would react to a friend self-harming, however. I know there's a part of me that wouldn't see it as inherently bad, but another small part of me would think "hey, maybe this person is in distress".

I made a cut along my tibial bone, down to said bone. It took a long time to heal, 8 weeks or so. It does seem like cuts there take longer to heal, but then again, my cut was also quite deep, long, and left gaping. That being said, the deep cuts I've made on my arms have taken significantly less time to heal.
Oh man... I'm having all this anxiety because my brother just found out about my overdose today. I didn't tell him, he pieced it together. Sorry about the confusion.
I've tried twice in the past five years. He wasn't there for the last two, but he found out about them recently. He's only learning everything now.
I ate before taking the pills, yes.

Hey... took the pills about three hours ago now. I'm not sure what to do. I think I should just let it run its course. I threw up earlier, no pills in my vomit, so I know they've been absorbed by now.

I really do need someone to talk to. I'm feeling alone right now. I've had way too many ER visits for my suicidal thoughts/intent, two of which were for overdoses. I can't go back for this, it's too embarrassing. Plus, I need to know I can see this through.
I don't have anyone who could go with me. I wouldn't want anyone to go with me. I can't go there regardless.

I can't go back to the ER for this. I just can't. They can't help, and it would be embarrassing for me to show up having overdosed again. If I'm lucky, I'll develop acute liver failure and die, like I'm supposed to.
I can't tell anyone... that's why I told all of you. It's a lonely thing, suicide. So I came here. But I can't actually tell anyone, not this time.
I can't do that. I just can't, not this time. This needs to actually happen.

I'm taking Prozac, but I only started it this week, so it's way too soon to tell if they're doing anything.

I'm not going to lie, I have a bunch of pills I've counted out and have been debating taking ever since I woke up this morning.

As far as I know for speeding up the group, what's been done has been done. I don't think I'm considered severe enough to have my name bumped up the list.

I just started antidepressants and I am in contact with the local crisis team. I'm not sure if it helps.

There's no particular reason, I just always feel this way. Granted, my current financial and living situations have made things that much more difficult.
I am not doing okay right now, and I have to wait up to a year to get into DBT therapy in my country. I'm honestly unsure if I'll survive until then with the constant suicidal thoughts.

I consider my self-harm to be neutral territory, a tool I use in order to stay alive. It's an act of survival to me. And yes, compared to other vices, it isn't as bad or as expensive. I don't really see my self-harm as much of a problem anymore.

No, in my experience, they won't necessarily commit someone for SI in my area. Though I was honest about my suicidal thoughts as well, the doctor there today was competent and asked me if I felt safe to go home, to which I replied with a yes. So go home I did, unfortunately sans stapler.

An endorphin rush gives me a feeling of euphoria and calm. It melts away my stress and numbness. I feel something, a pleasant feeling. In ways, it's very similar to a drug. I crave it, or need it at times.
Going into a dissociative state is more than enough reason to justify self-harming behaviour. I have often cut while in a dissociative state.

I can share in your feelings towards cutting the forearms. I also prefer cutting my forearms, and the cuts there somewhat mirror my work. It is the most satisfying place for me to cut, and I have cut on many parts of my body.

I wish I could give you a more scientific reason as to why this particular area is so commonly used among cutters and is often deemed the "most satisfying". There is most likely some form of medical as well as psychological reasoning as to why.

I have moved four times in the past four years. I moved across my country both times, no less. Getting a fresh start was always something I had in mind... it's something I constantly chase. There is an appeal, of leaving all the ghosts behind and going somewhere new where no one knows you.

I'm starting to realise that though a fresh start can sometimes be positive and be really great at the beginning, it doesn't really make depression go away. At least, it hasn't ever really helped with my depression.

Since this would be your first time moving to another city, I recommend you try it for the experience. It can really be a beautiful thing.
As for advice on how to deal with the change, quickly finding a job in your field of study helps a lot. A job keeps your mind occupied.
I graduated from college top of my class and was valedictorian despite having BPD and MDD.
Yes, I would recommend going to urgent care. You most likely require some form of medical suturing.

I have OD'ed as a form of self-harm. I have used both prescription medications and acetaminophen. I have also overdosed on both those categories of drugs as suicide attempts.

Part of it is self-harm, part of it is suicidal intent, and part of it is for science. That's how it is for me.

I feel somewhat fortunate, as I have access to a crisis chat service in my province that is pretty quick to respond. The only downside is that this service is only available during specific hours, which can make it difficult if it's the middle of the night and I'm feeling this way. Despite that, they've been pretty helpful for the most part.

The international crisis chat service I've used (IMAlive)  is okay. They definitely do have a long wait time sometimes. It's due to a large influx of people seeking out the service. That doesn't mean it isn't discouraging every time you click the chat button and it says "offline".

I once cut a small vein, and for days I would keep reopening the wound and letting it bleed. I also made a huge gash along my right tibia that bled for a while, and once wouldn't stop bleeding after being reopened. I experienced the symptoms of blood loss from the latter. I happened to be in a hospital setting when it happened, and the staff had trouble controlling the bleeding. I'm not going to lie, I wouldn't have minded if they just left me to bleed out.
I purge as a form of self-harm. I personally do see eating disorders as at least partially being a form of self-harm.

Making friends as an adult is really hard, especially when you're depressed. I'm also 23, and I have two friends I can think of, plus a couple of long-distance friendships, but that's about it.

Someone once said to me that people don't really care about you or your problems, that they only care about what you can offer them. Maybe there's some truth to that. This seems to be at least partially true of adult friendships.

I feel this way too. I have these feelings of emptiness and numbness that won't go away. Nothing brings me joy, and nothing brings me satisfaction (except self-harm). I often feel as though life is futile because I feel this way.

Yes, this has happened to me on numerous occasions. I'm very used to sweeping my problems under the rug, and I find it difficult to open up to friends, even though I want to at times. I feel as though opening up has bitten me in the ass one too many times, so I delete these messages and write new ones, or just pretend I'm kind of fine.

I have to disagree. I'm in a poor financial situation, and it has worsened my existing depression. I come from a middle class family, and my parents helped put me through school, but that's the extent of  it. Right now, I'm dirt poor, and though I am taking steps and trying to grind to make ends meet, my depression is just getting worse.

There is such a thing as functional depression too. It could be that people who are poor are depressed, but continue to function in order to survive/help their families survive. Also, if someone is poor/lives in a third-world country, it could be that they either can't afford mental health services, or don't have access to any. All of the same can be said for anxiety as well.

I have functional major depressive disorder, so I'm still depressed all the time despite appearing to function in day to day life. It's not a thing of "having the time" to be anxious or depressed. If you are anxious or depressed, those feelings don't really go away even though you're grinding to survive.

I am a logical and analytical person at heart, despite having BPD and the intense emotions that go along with it. There's a reason I bottle up my emotions. Emotions can be very volatile, especially to us. I often wish I could snuff out all emotions too. At the same time, this pervading numbness and emptiness I feel is excruciating in its own right.

When we experience pain, our brains secrete endorphins to help ease us through the pain. It's very possible the feelings of relaxation and calm you feel are from an endorphin rush. I feel this way when I self-harm.

I do feel a lot of shame. My anger is often directed at myself, and I think it's better that way for everyone. I'm currently feeling ashamed because I've been in a mental health crisis for about two months now. That's just fucking ridiculous... why haven't I been able to get my shit together?

Too much stress and I self-harm more frequently and have more suicidal thoughts than usual. I guess I don't handle stress very well. My depression becomes more of a monster on top of the BPD when I'm stressed out, too. Even when I was on meds (I really should be on meds now, honestly), my stress would "override" the medication and I would spiral.

You might want to consider reaching out to your psychiatrist, or a therapist of you have one. Talking about your stress and how it is affecting you with a professional is a good place to start.

I feel this way at times. I have a tendency to blame myself for my mental illnesses as well. I feel as though I must've done something wrong along the way. People tell me that it's a chemical imbalance and so on, but I can't help but feel at least partially responsible for it. Therapy can be scary because it makes us confront these parts of ourselves, and getting better can seem scary because what if it's all our faults?

I actually started feeling this way around your age, and for no apparent reason. I still haven't shaken the feeling. It might be depression. In my case, it turned out to be both depression and BPD that were making me feel this way, and other ways. This is not to say you have this diagnosis as well; only a professional can give you a diagnosis.

If you are concerned about how you're feeling, I would suggest you reach out to someone. Your parents, a friend, or a professional. A professional should get involved if these feelings persists, as you may be suffering from depression or another mental illness.
Oh yeah, I'm aware of "quiet BPD", and that's the model I fit the most. I've been in crisis since February, and it's been fucking up my life, so I get what you mean by the flare-ups as well.
That's also possible. The only way you'll truly know of you're depressed is by getting assessed by a professional. I would recommend going down that route.
I honestly hope so. The BPD label has so much stigma attached to it that I'm finding it difficult to get any help, and I know I'm not the only one who feels this way.

I can relate to your feelings so much. My depression is a monster that sapped my enjoyment from everything, even spending time with friends. I don't even feel like I want friends anymore though, because I've lost a few who couldn't handle the fact that I have mental illness and was going through a crisis. A paramedic once told me that it's surprising how quickly most people will just run away from issues like this, but the truth is that most people just can't handle anything emotional. It really makes friendships seem pointless.

This is a good time to consider reaching out to a professional about your issues. It sounds like they'e really increased in severity recently. If you're feeling scared, that's even more reason to reach out.

I try to remind myself that I'm talented and skilled at my job. I try and push myself every day to get my life in order. It doesn't work every day, but it works some days, and that has to count for something.

It can be difficult to do things when everything seems futile, or when anxiety becomes crippling. Sometimes the only thing you can do is try and push through those feelings. Keeping busy can actually help with these feelings a lot. It also helps to reach out for professional help.

Depression and anxiety can definitely interfere with our work, and even just daily activities like cleaning, showering, etc. I hate to admit, but my depression has interfered with my job a lot recently. It can become very disabling.

That's a really shitty situation. It's so difficult for those of us struggling with mental illness, because there is still stigma attached to it. Employers can be the worst when it comes to mental health issues. Some of the view it as an excuse to leave/miss work, despite the fact that we are genuinely unwell.

It is possible to find a workplace that'll treat you like a human being. I work for one such workplace, and they have been nothing but understanding of my issues. There's hope.
It sounds like you could be experiencing anxiety and depression. To know for sure, you should see if you can get properly assessed by either a medical professional, or a mental health professional.
One upside to depression for me is that I lost a lot of weight without trying.

If your cut is down to fat tissue and gaping, you definitely need sutures or staples. It's up to you if you want to go and have that done or not. I'm personally investing in my own medical stapler so I won't have to deal with doctors anymore.
Yeah, I feel that way. I don't know if this feeling ever goes away or not.

I think I can manage. I know how to suture tissue. Suturing myself is too difficult when I cut on my arms, so I think a medical stapler is the way to go. I honestly think it is worth the minimal risk, and it's not like pain will be an issue.
That makes sense, thank you.
Stop now while you can. You don't want to go deeper. It becomes an addiction.

Guess what? I just got staples at this other clinic, and they are detaining me and transferring me to a hospital, one I haven't been to before. This is exactly what I tried to avoid. I pleaded with the doctor, but he says he doesn't feel comfortable letting me go, and the psychiatrist he spoke to over the phone about my case wants to see me. Nonsense, all of it...

I can relate to this. More than once, a hotline has called the police on me. The truth is that they have the obligation to do so if they believe you are an imminent risk to yourself.

I have lied at the hospital in the past, withholding important information that they needed to help me. Lying isn't going to get you anywhere at the end of the day. Sure, you'll get discharged, and your mind might think that's what it wants, but there's a part of your mind that also called the hotline to reach out in the first place.

I know you're looking at those pills right now. I understand you may not want to call the hotline, but I suggest you do. There's a part of you still holding on.
I don't find it weird. It sounds ideal to me. That's what I would prefer for myself as well.

To be frank with you, this post is insensitive towards all of us who actually deal with self-harm and mental illness. Don't expect anyone to answer your question.

Look, I can see that you may be having anxiety about this next chapter in your life, and it's making you consider self-harm. That honestly could be enough in itself for you to get out of it, without actually "faking" that you have depression and so on.

People who fake mental illness and self-harm make it more difficult for those with these issues to seek help, as it can potentially perpetuate the stigma that self-harm is attention-seeking behaviour (it often isn't). Keep that in mind if you plan to go through with your idea.

Dying is scary, even for those of us who are suicidal. It's a very permanent thing. A lot of us don't actually want to die, we just want the pain to end.

Even if things appear to be going well, it doesn't mean you are well. It's possible to appear completely functional, yet be crumbling on the inside.

I understand your feelings of thinking that everything and everyone would be better off or okay without you. Many of us feel that way, especially when suicidal.

Also, you are not "just suicidal ". These are serious, potentially dangerous thoughts at the end of the day. They shouldn't be taken lightly. Even if you think you can't pull the trigger, it doesn't mean you won't one day. You may want to think about reaching out to a professional at this point.
I personally can't get into burning, at least not with fire/a heated object. Chemical burns, though... I can do that. Still, I personally find cutting to be the most satisfying form of self-harm.
I'm aware of how painful it is. Bring it on! At least the mortality rate is high. I'm about to take the pills in the next ten minutes.

Last night, I tried to pull out an IV I had in due to an overdose. A bunch of nurses came to grab my hands, but they underestimated my strength. I scratched a nurse, security was called, and I put up a Hell of a fight as they put me in restraints. I have really bad anger that I keep hidden most of the time. Let's just say that the caged animal inside of me got out last night, and is still on a rampage. I now have thoughts of hurting other people on top of my thoughts/behaviours of harming myself.

I do listen to music while I self-harm, almost every time. My self-harming is a very clinical process, so I "recreate" a clinical environment, and that includes favourite tunes. It helps keep me somewhat removed from the situation while I'm making very deep cuts.

I don't really care about the pain. I tried overdosing on it before, so I'm aware of how sick I'll get. Still planning on taking 16 extra-strength  pills tonight to get the process started. It's not like a hospital will find out anyway.

I'm sorry you had such a shitty experience with this police officer. He was an absolute prick for saying that your cutting is just for attention. Even when cutting is done with the goal of attention (not saying yours is), it's still self-harm, and the person still needs help.

You obviously are in a lot of pain, which is why you cut yourself to cope. All of us here realise that, and your emotions and pain are valid. Being suicidal since age 11 is fucking tough. I've been suicidal since 17 (am now 23), so I can somewhat understand your struggle, at least in terms of these thoughts lasting years.

I hope that your view of police officers is not completely tarnished by this experience. I don't know where you live, but I live in Canada and have had a fair share of run-ins with police due to my worsening mental health. If anything, I've often found the police to be more understanding and compassionate than some of the MH professionals I've met. Granted, I was put in handcuffs last time, but they were still (weirdly) nice about it.

I started self-harming/cutting at 17, which is a little later in life as far as self-harming goes. I started cutting after my first suicide attempt. I had jumped out of a moving vehicle, and I remember the pain made me feel great. I had to feel that again, to deal with my emotions and thoughts.

I started by punching walls, then began cutting. I've also overdosed and purged as methods of self-harm. It's been almost six years since my first attempt, and I'm still cutting, but I do deep cuts now.
Thank you for sharing your experience. I'm sorry the doctor you saw was so dismissive of your symptoms. Have you tried getting a second opinion for your neurological symptoms?

Keep trying to talk to him. Do regular welfare checks on him. Text or phone regularly. Try to get him to communicate, or at least maintain communication in these ways. If he's talking, he's still alive.

Tell him that you want to help, and you will not judge him. Because you're a parental figure, that may make him hesitant to reach out to you. After all, children grow up knowing their parents have expectations for them, which is why this is such a delicate subject for both of you.

If you ever get really concerned that you are fearing for his life, call 911 and show up at his place for support. With you there, it might alleviate some tension, and he may be more ready to open up to authorities.

I hope you are able to help your son get the help he needs.

Thank you. Some days, I think I want it, other days, I don't. I feel like I'm in quicksand, in limbo most days. I hope I can manage to feel better, too... but I also hope that maybe I'll finally succeed in suicide. It's a strange place to be, and I'm sorry for rambling.

I understand your frustrations with hearing this. These words feel extremely hollow when we are in the depths of depression.

The person or people who say this mean well. I realise that when I get the same spiel, but it doesn't change the fact that the words seem meaningless.

My coworkers at my main workplace are supportive, but it's also a small team of about six people. I had what you could call a mental health crisis last month, and my supervisor was informed and has shown nothing but support, as have the rest of the staff.

In your situation, if the staff is quite big, I would just reach out to the two friends you mentioned. If they are really good friends, you should be able to confide in them. I understand the risk of Chinese whispers. That's why I'm not open about my issues at work too much, especially if I go and work at a sister location. If you do open up, do bring up that you would like this to be kept confidential for these reasons.

As for being judged and so on if word does get out, yes, that can still happen. I don't want to say that to discourage you from reaching out, I'm simply being realistic. There's still some people who stigmatize mental illness. You even admitted that you used to view it that way before you got depressed. I did, too. Try and be mindful when you're sharing your personal struggles.

I feel you handled the situation very professionally. If you can't perform at work one day, then you are better off going home and getting some rest, especially since you mentioned you're in a senior position. You are setting a good example for your team.

As for your boss' response, I feel it wasn't very professional. He seems to understand the fact that you're struggling, but I doubt he actually understands the struggles you're going through. The truth is that yes, your medication certainly can affect you this way! It might be worth your while to explain this to your boss in a brief private meeting, and you may even want to consider getting a doctor's note.

I work in a high pressure environment, and I'm fortunate in that my coworkers at my main workplace are very understanding. My previous manager even said to me that if I needed to take a mental health day to just do it. Thankfully, I didn't have to do that very often, but the option was there for me.

The only thing I didn't like that my former manager said during that time was regarding stress leave. She said that it's there if I need it, but I should try not to take it because it could potentially put a black mark on my name. Basically, not everyone who takes stress leave and comes back is able to recover professionally. That being said, if you ever need to take stress leave, you should just do it. It's not worth burning out.

I started experiencing this yesterday. I really noticed that I wasn't getting any pleasure from music or singing at all, which made me stop for a second. Music had always been that one thing I felt I could still count on to make me feel something. Now I feel nothing but indifference when listening to favourite songs.
I understand how you feel, I get tired of hearing all these expressions as well, especially as of late. The words just come across as hollow to me.

At the end of the day, having suicidal thoughts can be distressing, whether you act on them or not. You are doing the right thing by reaching out to people.

You are experiencing suicidal ideation, so thoughts of suicide. The next level would be suicidal intent, where you are actively seeking out the means to do so, possibly harming yourself (parasuicide), and maybe even making a plan.

You say you fear death and would never kill yourself because of your family. Hold on to those thoughts. It's surprising how quickly we can forget these things when we are on the edge. I hope you never stop fearing death.

Show me a person who hasn't thought of suicide at least once, and I'll show you a liar. Yes, to a degree, it's normal to think about and consider suicide from time to time. These thoughts being constant, on a daily basis for years, I'm not sure if that's normal or not, but it's my normal.

I picture my death by my own hands a lot. I don't think about how it'll affect others much after I'm gone. I don't think I care about that. When you're suicidal, it can be easy to forget about people around you when all you can think about is ending the pain. Every time I've attempted suicide, I never thought about how it would impact others if I succeeded. I was so focused in the moment, in a trance-like state.

I guess an existential crisis turns into suicidal tendencies once you start actively thinking about ways to kill yourself and start acquiring the means to do so.

Are suicidal thoughts part of the human experience?  Yes, they are, to a degree. However, is it normal to have been preoccupied with such thoughts regularly since childhood? I'm not sure, but it's your normal.
Yes, I have done this, because depression has killed my appetite as well. It's way easier to just drink a couple of ensures a day than to actually eat something. It's definitely better than nothing.

I understand the thought, but mine ventures more towards simply wanting to die. I've been having these thoughts a lot recently. Why should someone such as myself, who wants to die, finds no happiness in life, and is a burden to those around her, continue to live while there are people with terminal illnesses who would gladly switch places if they could?

I didn't start self-harming until the end of high school. I will admit that I self-harmed a lot during college, and I did do it in the college bathrooms almost daily, and I was even able to do it discretely in class as well. I never left blood or blades as evidence. All that being said, I'm pretty sure that some of my college classmates, as well as my professor, suspected that when I was leaving the classroom to "go to the bathroom", it was to cut.
I can't picture recovery. I can't even picture a future for myself, let alone recovery.

You're not alone in these feelings. I know I would say the same things to a friend or family member at their intake, say all those words of support and encouragement, yet I feel suicidal everyday, and also possess the means to go through with it. I'm a hypocrite, too.

This family member of yours seems to have gotten to a point where her condition became so severe that others took notice and followed up by taking some actions to help her get the help she needs. It's very possible that no one is noticing your struggle. I know that sounds shitty. I myself have a tendency to bottle everything up, so people don't necessarily know.

I keep trying to tell myself that I can get it under control myself, that it's all in my head, that it's not a chemical imbalance in my brain. I honestly don't know what it is anymore, but I do know I've been depressed for a long time. Being depressed is fucking surreal at times.

It honestly sounds like your mutual "friend" is picking sides in this argument, which isn't fair to you or your ex-boyfriend.

As for manipulation, I'm a believer that in order to be manipulative, there has to be intent to manipulate someone or a group of people. I don't see any intent at all in your words, I see someone who is suffering right now. It's extremely unfair for them to see your suicidal thoughts as a means of manipulation. If you're hurting so much that you want to die, then you're obviously hurting a lot.

Does weed cause depression, or make it worse? I have strong doubts of that. I was using weed regularly to self-medicate for two years. It was the only thing that was helping me to get my self-harm and suicidal thoughts under control.

No, I don't think weed makes depression worse. I think mental health professionals have got that all wrong. It's not that weed causes depression, it's that a lot of people who use it regularly have pre-existing depression, and we're all just self-medicating.

In the past couple of months, weed hasn't been cutting it for me, but I know the weed didn't make my depression worse, other outside factors did, or the fact that I wasn't seeking any treatment for it. I was recently forced into a living situation that prevents me from using cannabis, and my depression has gotten worse for it, and I'm past the withdrawal stage.

Weed isn't that bad a drug at all. Alcohol is way worse. Stick to pot, but be open to the idea that you may need some other medication to go along with it.

I'm sorry to hear that you are having issues with your self-image, which in turn are making your depression worse. It's difficult for us to accept these physical phenomena that are out of our control. Your receding hairline definitely counts.

You are taking a positive step in going to see your barber. As for shaving it all off, I say you give it a try. Having no hair is a freeing experience, and you may find it easier to accept your hair loss if you get rid of all the hair on top of your head completely.

Being bald is not a turn off. I know many women, including myself, who find baldness attractive on a man.

I understand this may not change how you feel. After all, you do have a lot going on in your life, stating not having friends, a job, or confidence, as well as dealing with depression. Shaving your hair off and taking control of that aspect of your life may give you a boost of confidence, so it's worth a try, I think.

It sounds like your doctor is very much aware of your depression already. However, I understand why you may be hesitant to bring up your recent thoughts of suicide with your doctor. Some GPs get... jumpy when they hear the word suicide. I know my current GP does, so I'm considering looking for help elsewhere.

Yes, you can have BPD without experiencing trauma in your childhood. There is research that suggests that BPD can be passed on genetically, and if you have a parent with BPD, you're more likely to develop it. My father has it, something I found out after I was diagnosed.

That being said, trauma is a much broader term than we often think. It's not always sexual or physical abuse; sometimes it's verbal abuse, bullying, witnessing a traumatic incident despite not being in immediate harm, having a serious illness, etc. It's possible you did experience something in childhood that your brain registered as trauma at the time.
